analysis.one_liner: Bars states from taxing companies that sell into the state without a physical presence there.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on May 4, 2006 and never received a vote before the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite a 1959 federal law that limits when states can tax out-of-state businesses. It would stop states from imposing income, gross-receipts, or franchise taxes on any company unless that company has employees or property physically located in the state, and it would extend that shield beyond physical goods to services, intangible property, and software. A company could sell into a state freely and pay that state nothing in business taxes.
analysis.who_benefits: Large multistate companies — national retailers, mail-order and internet sellers, service firms, and software licensors — that sell into states where they have no employees, offices, or property. They would owe no state income or business-activity taxes in those states, cutting their tax bills and giving them a price advantage over local businesses that do pay.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the federal prohibition on state business taxes to out-of-state transactions involving all forms of property, including intangibles and services — not just sales of tangible personal goods.

Prohibits any state from imposing a business tax on an out-of-state entity unless that entity has a physical presence in the state, defined mainly as more than 21 days of employee activity, an exclusive agent, or owned or leased property.
Extends the shield beyond net income taxes to gross-receipts, franchise, capital-stock, and other business-activity taxes, the main ways states tax companies that don't fit the income-tax mold.
Excludes licensed computer software from the definition of tangible personal property, so software owners selling licenses into a state would not create a taxable presence there.

analysis.who_pays: State and local governments, which would lose revenue from business-activity taxes on interstate commerce — meaning residents either lose services or make up the difference through other taxes. In-state businesses would also face competition from out-of-state rivals selling the same goods and services tax-free.

drawbacks.text: States would lose tax revenue on interstate business activity conducted inside their borders, forcing cuts to services or higher taxes on residents and in-state firms to make up the difference.
It creates an uneven playing field: a local business selling the same product or service pays the state's business taxes, while an out-of-state competitor selling into the same market pays nothing.

The bill keeps a few carve-outs — states could still tax live performances and sporting events before audiences of more than 100, and could pursue enforcement against sham transactions — but those cover a small slice of interstate commerce.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real simplification argument: national companies today navigate thousands of overlapping local tax rules, and a bright-line physical-presence test is easier to comply with. But the savings flow almost entirely to large multistate firms, while the revenue loss lands on state budgets that fund schools, roads, and services, and the competitive imbalance favors the biggest national players over local businesses. Sales and use taxes are expressly left alone, so the largest revenue question — collecting sales tax on remote sales — was not even addressed by this bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2006, sent to the Senate Finance Committee the same day, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. Charles Schumer introduced the bill on May 4, 2006, joined by five cosponsors — five Republicans and one Democrat.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action appears in the record: no committee markup, no floor vote, no House action before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State and local governments kept their full authority to tax business activity conducted in their states, and in-state businesses were not put at a tax disadvantage against untaxed out-of-state competitors. The multistate companies the bill was written for did not gain the exemption.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State and local governments and local businesses

sides.party_line_note: A Democratic senator introduced the bill with five Republican cosponsors; because no vote ever occurred, no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Multistate retailers, mail-order and internet sellers, and software licensors
industries.note: The bill would exempt them from state income, gross-receipts, and franchise taxes in any state where they lack a physical presence, sharply cutting their tax bills on remote sales. The public cost is lost state revenue and an unfair advantage over taxed local competitors.

The bill would strip states of the power to tax most out-of-state business activity, reducing the revenue that funds schools, roads, and services. Residents would bear the difference through cuts or other taxes.

The bill offers them no relief: they would keep paying state business taxes while untaxed out-of-state rivals sell into the same market. The bill's simplification benefits go to the largest multistate firms, not to them.
